name: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle
statement: The more precisely you fix a particle's position, the less its momentum can be defined.
statementAccent: the less its momentum can be defined
meaning: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle holds that certain pairs of physical properties, called conjugate variables, cannot both be defined to arbitrary precision at the same time. For the most famous pair, position and momentum, the product of the two uncertainties has a nonzero lower bound: the spread in position times the spread in momentum is at least the reduced Planck constant divided by two. Crucially this is not a limit on our instruments but an intrinsic feature of quantum states themselves, which simply do not possess sharply defined values of both quantities at once. It is one of the deepest and most misunderstood results in all of physics.
mechanism: The principle follows from the wave nature of matter. A quantum state's descriptions in position and in momentum are Fourier transforms of one another, and a function sharply peaked in one representation is necessarily spread out in the other, so localising a particle in space forces its momentum to fan out. Formally, the position and momentum operators do not commute, their commutator being the imaginary unit times the reduced Planck constant, and non-commuting observables cannot share a common set of definite-valued states. Werner Heisenberg's original 1927 argument used a gamma-ray microscope thought experiment and gave only an order-of-magnitude relation; Earle Kennard and Hermann Weyl then supplied the rigorous inequality in terms of standard deviations.

examples.text: The canonical pair: the product of the spreads in a particle's position and momentum cannot be smaller than about half the reduced Planck constant, no matter how the state is prepared.

A wave passing a narrow slit has a well-defined position there but spreads out in angle beyond it; narrowing the slit sharpens position and widens the diffraction, trading one uncertainty for the other.
Because a particle cannot have both a definite position and zero momentum, quantum systems retain a minimum energy even at absolute zero, such as the residual energy of a harmonic oscillator.

variants.name: The Robertson-Schrodinger relation
variants.text: The general form bounding the uncertainties of any two observables by their commutator, of which the position-momentum relation is the famous special case.

variants.name: The energy-time relation
variants.text: A related inequality tying the spread in energy to a characteristic time, but with a different logical status, since time is a parameter in quantum mechanics rather than an observable.

whyItMatters: The uncertainty principle is a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, marking a fundamental break from the classical assumption that a particle has, at every instant, a definite position and momentum waiting to be measured. It underlies zero-point energy, the stability and size of atoms, the natural width of spectral lines, and the very limits of what can be known about a physical system. More broadly, it reshaped the philosophy of science, replacing a deterministic clockwork universe with one in which certain complementary properties are, at bottom, not simultaneously definite.

working.lead: Trade one precision for the other
working.text: when position is pinned down, expect momentum to become correspondingly ill-defined, and the reverse.

working.lead: Read it as a property of nature
working.text: treat the limit as intrinsic to the quantum state, not as a shortcoming of measuring equipment that better tools could beat.
understand the conjugate quantity as genuinely undefined, not merely hidden, unlike ordinary classical ignorance.

limits: The principle constrains only specific conjugate pairs, not every quantity, so individual observables can each be known precisely, just not both members of a conjugate pair at once. The rigorous position-momentum bound is a statement about the intrinsic statistical spread of a state, distinct from the separate relation describing how a measurement disturbs a system, and conflating the two has caused lasting confusion. The energy-time form is legitimate but rests on subtler foundations, since time is not an operator in the ordinary theory. And the precise bound is the reduced Planck constant over two, which Heisenberg's original heuristic argument, giving only an order-of-magnitude relation, did not itself establish.
misreadings: It is not merely the observer effect, the idea that measuring disturbs the system; the rigorous principle is about the intrinsic spread of quantum states and holds even for perfect instruments, since no state violating it can even be prepared. It is not measurement error or instrument limitation. It does not say everything is uncertain, only that specific conjugate pairs cannot be sharp together. And the precise one-half-times-reduced-Planck bound comes from Kennard and Weyl, not from Heisenberg's original microscope argument, which gave only a rough relation.
origin: Introduced by Werner Heisenberg in a 1927 paper in Zeitschrift fur Physik, where he argued it semi-quantitatively via a microscope thought experiment; Earle Kennard gave the rigorous inequality the same year, and Howard Robertson generalised it in 1929.
